newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Airlines see record profit but dangers loom.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Airlines see record profit but dangers loom.

text.p: International airlines were on Monday reportedly heading for record profits this year but facing growing problems from soaring fuel prices and mounting costs imposed by government and airport authorities.

Pierre Jeanniot, Director-General of the industry's global body IATA, told its annual general meeting that the balance of income over expenditure from the more than 250 member carriers this year should reach $5.5 billion.

"On revenues of $128.8 billion, that represents only four percent. It may not seem very high, but in dollar terms, it is still an all-time record," said Jeanniot in a state-of-the- industry report to IATA airline executives.

But the IATA chief and other top aviation officials warned the climb over the past three years out of the recession in the early 1990s, when airlines notched up total losses of $15.2 billion, could easily turn into a nose-dive.

Major concerns included fuel prices, which account for between 10 and 20 percent of the costs of IATA members, and charges for airport use and air traffic control services, which account for some 10 percent of operating costs.
He attributed the drop in potential profits this year from the $6 billion he predicted in April mostly to these factors.

Jeanniot said the some 15-percent fuel hike since last year, given extra impetus by the firing of 27 Cruise missiles against Iraq by United States warjets in September, had not yet reached crisis stage.
But if the rise continued, it would rapidly eat into the airlines' new profitability, hitting at plans to update fleets with more efficient and environmentally-friendly aircraft.

At a news conference later, Jeanniot and top officials of the German airline Deutsche Lufthansa AG and Swissair indicated the rises would almost inevitably be passed on in the shape of all-around higher prices to passengers.
IATA has called an emergency meeting for November 13 in Geneva on the issue.

Jeanniot, former chief of Air Canada, said there was a growing consensus among airlines, many of whom in Europe have already hiked charges for travellers and freight, that part of the higher costs would have to be born by travellers.
"There is a limit to how much can be absorbed by the airlines," he declared.
Lufthansa chairman Juergen Weber said his company, which has already raised cargo charges, would also hike passenger prices during the month. But the amount would vary from area to area.

Earlier, Otto Loepfe, president IATA and Swissair, told the annual general meeting that airlines must also fight unfair price fixing policies set by monopolies providing many of the services they needed.
"All our airlines have one thing in common. We are not making enough money," he said.

The service monopolies bore a large part of the blame, he said. "From their privileged position, and often encouraged by the states they serve, they charge fees for their services that hit and hurt all of us so much that they seriously threaten our long-term survival," Loepfe said.

Jeanniot also addressed another key industry issue when he warned the meeting that a rush by carriers into hastily-conceived alliances to capture a bigger chunk of the booming market could bring problems if not well thought out.

Around the world, nearly 200 commercial airlines currently had a total of some 200 alliances, less than one-fifth involving equity sharing but at least one-third covering code-sharing or joint operation of flights.

"There is no doubt that the airlines are trying to give better service, but the rush to create mega-networks without clearly defined synergies can lead to an unstable, randomly-assembled set of arrangements," he said.
